parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Falls prevention and care after a fall
blurb: Apply NICE NG249 to decide who gets a comprehensive falls assessment, what it includes, and how to act after a fall with a head injury.
question: Mrs Price, 83, takes apixaban. At 03:00 she is found on the floor beside her bed. She says she hit her head but cannot remember falling. Her GCS is 15 and she has not vomited. What should the nurse do after checking her for injuries?

teach.body: NICE NG249 (April 2025) replaced CG161. It covers people aged 65 and over, and people aged 50 to 64 who are at higher risk of falling because of an underlying condition. Its biggest change: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Plain English: stop scoring people to decide who deserves help. In hospital and residential care, everyone in scope is offered a comprehensive falls assessment and management, and in the community the person's falls history decides the route.

teach.text: Falls risk SCORES are out. NG249 rec 1.1.1: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict risk. A low score never excuses an inpatient from a comprehensive falls assessment; every inpatient in scope gets one.

teach.h: Community: which route after asking about falls?

children.label: Comprehensive assessment and management
children.sub: Frailty, injury needing treatment, loss of consciousness, could not get up, 2+ falls

teach.caption: NG249 recs 1.1.2–1.1.6. Ask opportunistically, for example at annual reviews.

head: Area
What it includes

Gait, balance, strength, feet and footwear, neuro exam
Alcohol, diet, fluids and weight loss
Functional ability and fear of falling

steps.label: Lying
steps.sub: Measure BP lying (or seated if lying is impractical)

steps.label: Stand
steps.sub: Measure again after at least 1 minute standing

steps.label: Compare
steps.sub: Systolic fall 20+ or diastolic fall 10+ is significant

teach.caption: NICE NG136 recs 1.1.5–1.1.8; part of the NG249 cardiovascular examination.

teach.h: Managing falls risk on the ward
teach.body: In hospital, tailor interventions to the person: which risk factors can be improved during the stay, which risks come from the ward environment, and education the person can engage with. Consider adjusting medicines as part of a structured medication review. Reassure people they can still get up and help them dress, stand and walk regularly. There is insufficient evidence for vitamin D specifically to reduce falls in hospital, but people are encouraged to follow NHS vitamin D advice for bone and muscle health. At discharge, consider referral to community services.

teach.h: Head injury after a fall (NICE NG232, adults)
head: Situation
CT head
rows: GCS 12 or less, seizure, focal deficit, vomiting more than once
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet (not aspirin alone), no other indication
Same, presenting more than 8 hours after injury
Loss of consciousness or amnesia AND aged 65+
teach.caption: NG232 recs 1.5.8, 1.5.9, 1.5.13. Anticoagulants include DOACs, warfarin, heparin and LMWH.

teach.body: Mrs Price, 83, takes apixaban and is found on the floor by her bed. She says she hit her head but cannot remember falling. The nurse checks her for injury before moving her, following the ward post-fall protocol, takes a full set of observations with GCS, and escalates to the doctor because she is anticoagulated and has amnesia for the event: a CT head scan within 8 hours of the injury is indicated. She starts neurological observations, records the fall, reports the incident, informs her family and updates her falls plan.

items.label: CT on an anticoagulant with no other indication

items: Check for injury (head, hips, spine) before moving the person; use the local safe-lifting protocol.
Full observations with GCS; escalate if anticoagulated, head injury, new pain or deterioration.
Start neurological observations if there is a head injury.
Look for the cause: delirium, postural drop, infection, medicines, continence, environment.
Record, report the incident, tell the family and update the falls care plan.
NG249 covers people 65+, or 50–64 at higher risk; no falls risk prediction tools.
All inpatients and care home residents in scope: comprehensive falls assessment and management.
Community: comprehensive assessment if fallen in the last year plus frailty, injury needing treatment, loss of consciousness, unable to get up, or 2+ falls.
Lying and standing BP: a systolic fall of 20 or diastolic of 10 mmHg after 1 minute standing is significant.
Head injury on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet (not aspirin alone): consider CT within 8 hours.

summary: You can now decide who needs a comprehensive falls assessment under NICE NG249, list what it includes and carry out a lying and standing BP. You can also escalate correctly after a fall with a head injury in someone on an anticoagulant.

A.q: Which person falls within the scope of NICE NG249 falls guidance?
options: Ms Ade, 45, who fell and sprained an ankle at work
Mr Cho, 61, fit and active with no falls risk factors
Mr Bell, 58, with Parkinson's disease and a recent fall
Mrs Rose, 48, with mild asthma who tripped on a step outside
A.why: NG249 covers people 65 and over, and people 50 to 64 at higher risk of falling because of an underlying condition such as Parkinson's disease.

whyNot.0: At 45 she is under the age range of the guideline.
whyNot.1: People aged 50 to 64 are in scope when at higher risk; he has no risk factors.
whyNot.3: At 48 she is under the age range, and mild asthma is not a falls risk condition here.

A.q: Mr Hill, 80, has a lying and standing blood pressure check after a fall. Each standing reading was taken after 1 minute. Which pair of readings shows significant postural hypotension?
options: Lying 138/78, standing 124/72
Lying 138/78, standing 116/74
Lying 138/78, standing 130/70
Lying 138/78, standing 122/70
A.why: NICE NG136: a fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic of 10 mmHg or more, is significant. 138 to 116 is a 22 mmHg systolic fall.

whyNot.0: A 14 mmHg systolic and 6 mmHg diastolic fall are below the thresholds.
whyNot.2: An 8 mmHg fall in both systolic and diastolic is below the thresholds.
whyNot.3: A 16 mmHg systolic and 8 mmHg diastolic fall are below the thresholds.

A.q: A ward manager proposes using a falls risk score on admission so that only high-scoring patients have a full falls assessment. What does NICE NG249 say?
options: Use the score, then assess anyone scoring high
Use the score, alongside clinical judgement
Use the score weekly to track changes in each patient's risk
Offer every inpatient in scope a full assessment
A.why: NG249 rec 1.1.1: do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict risk; rec 1.1.7: offer everyone in hospital inpatient settings (in scope) a comprehensive falls assessment and management.

whyNot.0: NICE says do not use falls risk prediction tools, and assessment is for all inpatients in scope.
whyNot.1: Adding judgement does not change the advice: prediction tools are not used.
whyNot.2: Repeated scoring is still use of a prediction tool, which NICE advises against.

B.q: During a comprehensive falls assessment, Mr Rao, 79, describes the room spinning when he turns over in bed or looks up. Which assessment does NICE NG249 suggest considering?
options: A Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre
A Timed Up and Go test
A carotid sinus investigation
A 4-metre gait speed test
B.why: NG249 rec 1.2.2: ask about dizziness, and if the person reports rotational vertigo consider a Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre.

whyNot.1: Timed Up and Go measures mobility; it does not assess rotational vertigo.
whyNot.2: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is investigated for falls with an unexplained cause, not positional vertigo.
whyNot.3: Gait speed assesses frailty and mobility, not the cause of positional vertigo.

B.q: Mr Daly, 74, takes clopidogrel after a stroke. He slips on the ward and bumps his head. He is alert with a GCS of 15, has not vomited, and has no other indication for a CT scan. What does NICE NG232 advise?
options: Consider a CT head scan within 1 hour
Consider a CT head scan within 24 hours
Consider a CT head scan within 8 hours
Observe him, as antiplatelets are excluded
B.why: NG232 rec 1.5.13: with no other CT indication, people on anticoagulant or antiplatelet treatment (excluding aspirin monotherapy) should be considered for a CT head scan within 8 hours of the injury.

whyNot.0: Within 1 hour applies to the 1.5.8 risk factors, or if presenting more than 8 hours after injury.
whyNot.3: Only aspirin monotherapy is excluded; clopidogrel is included.

B.q: Mrs Gill, 81, fell twice during a 3-week admission. Her risk factors included dizziness on standing and night-time urgency. She is now going home. What does NICE NG249 suggest at discharge?
options: Give her a falls risk score to pass to her GP
Consider referral to community services for her risk factors
Advise her to rest at home until her follow-up review appointment
Start vitamin D tablets to prevent further falls
B.why: NG249 rec 1.3.16: at discharge, consider referring the person to community services so that risk factors identified in hospital that remain relevant at home can be addressed.

whyNot.0: NICE advises against falls risk prediction tools.
whyNot.2: NICE encourages activity; restricting activity is not advised.
whyNot.3: There is insufficient evidence for vitamin D to lower falls risk; NHS bone health advice applies instead.

C.q: Mrs Price, 83, takes apixaban. At 03:00 she is found on the floor by her bed. She says she hit her head but cannot remember falling. After injury checks she is helped back to bed: GCS 15, no vomiting, no neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Escalate for a CT head scan within 8 hours of the fall
Escalate for a CT head scan within 1 hour of the fall
Start hourly neurological observations and review at 08:00
Omit her morning apixaban and review on the ward round
C.why: She is on an anticoagulant (NG232 1.5.13) and is 65+ with amnesia since the injury (1.5.9): both point to a CT head scan within 8 hours of the injury. Neurological observations start as well, but escalation cannot wait.

whyNot.1: No 1-hour risk factor is present (GCS 15, no vomiting, seizure or deficit), and she presented within 8 hours.
whyNot.2: Observations alone miss the CT indication, and waiting until 08:00 delays escalation.
whyNot.3: Anticoagulant decisions are medical and do not replace urgent escalation for CT.

C.q: Mr Okoye, 77, takes warfarin. He tripped in his garden yesterday evening and bumped his head, and attends the emergency department 10 hours later. He has no other indication for a CT head scan. Within what time should a CT head scan be considered?
options: Within 8 hours of arrival
Within 24 hours of the injury
Within 4 hours of arrival
Within 1 hour of arrival
C.why: NG232 rec 1.5.13: on an anticoagulant with no other indication, consider CT within 8 hours of the injury, or within the hour if the person presents more than 8 hours after the injury.

whyNot.0: The 8-hour window runs from the injury; he presents after it, so the scan should be within the hour.
whyNot.1: 24 hours is not an NG232 time frame for this group.
whyNot.2: 4 hours is not the NG232 time frame; it is within 1 hour for a late presentation.

C.q: Mr Ellis, 76, has had three falls this year without tripping, warning or dizziness. His lying and standing BP is normal and his medicines have been reviewed. Which intervention does NICE NG249 recommend for falls with an unexplained cause?
options: A falls risk prediction score to grade his risk
Vitamin D supplements to reduce his falls risk
Investigation for carotid sinus hypersensitivity
Hip protectors and a bed alarm as the main part of his plan
C.why: NG249 rec 1.3.8: if falls have an unexplained cause, investigate possible cardioinhibitory carotid sinus hypersensitivity and consider cardiac pacing if indicated.

whyNot.0: NICE advises against falls risk prediction tools.
whyNot.1: NICE found insufficient evidence for vitamin D specifically to lower falls risk.
whyNot.3: Equipment does not address an unexplained, possibly cardiac, cause.

reteach.title: Assess the person, not a score
reteach.question: Why did NICE move away from falls risk scores towards a full assessment for every inpatient?

blocks.h: Risk factors are what you can fix
blocks.body: A score gives a number but changes nothing. NG249 asks for a comprehensive falls assessment that finds each person's own risk factors (a postural drop, delirium, a sleeping tablet, urgency at night, poor footwear) and then promptly addresses each one. In hospital, every inpatient in scope gets this.

blocks.text: On an anticoagulant or antiplatelet (other than aspirin alone) and a head injury: consider CT within 8 hours of the injury, even with GCS 15.

explain.body: NG249 covers people 65 and over, and those 50 to 64 at higher risk. Do not use falls risk prediction tools. Everyone in scope in hospital or residential care is offered a comprehensive falls assessment and management.

test.q: Which inpatients should be offered a comprehensive falls assessment under NICE NG249?
options: Those who score high on a validated falls risk prediction tool
Those who have fallen during this admission
Those with two or more falls in the last year
All inpatients aged 65 and over, or 50–64 at higher risk
test.why: NG249 rec 1.1.7 offers a comprehensive falls assessment and management to people in hospital inpatient settings within the guideline's scope.

whyNot.0: NICE advises against falls risk prediction tools.
whyNot.1: Assessment is offered on admission to all in scope, not after an inpatient fall.
whyNot.2: The 2-or-more criterion is for community settings; all inpatients in scope are offered it.

explain.body: Ask about falls opportunistically. Comprehensive assessment and management for people who fell in the last year and are living with frailty, were injured needing treatment, lost consciousness, could not get up independently, or had 2 or more falls. Otherwise assess gait and balance.

test.q: Mr Burns, 72, fell once at home last month. He was not hurt but lay on the floor for 2 hours because he could not get up. He is not frail. What does NICE NG249 recommend?
options: Health and wellbeing information and activity advice
A gait and balance assessment by itself
A comprehensive falls assessment and management
A falls risk score to decide on referral
test.why: NG249 rec 1.1.3: being unable to get up independently after a fall is one of the criteria for comprehensive falls assessment and management.

whyNot.0: Information and advice is for people with no falls, or one fall without gait or balance impairment and no criteria.
whyNot.1: Gait and balance assessment is for people without any rec 1.1.3 criteria; he has one.
whyNot.3: NICE advises against falls risk prediction tools.

explain.body: Alcohol, cardiovascular examination with lying and standing BP, cognition and mood, delirium (inpatients and care homes), diet and fluids, dizziness, feet and footwear, functional ability and fear of falling, gait, balance and strength, hearing, long-term conditions, medication review, neurological examination, osteoporosis risk, continence and vision.

test.q: Which element does NICE NG249 include in the comprehensive falls assessment for hospital inpatients but not for people in community settings?
options: Medication review
Assessment for delirium
Urinary continence
Lying and standing blood pressure
test.why: NG249 rec 1.2.2 includes delirium assessment for hospital inpatient and residential care settings only.

whyNot.0: Medication review is part of the assessment in all settings.
whyNot.2: Urinary continence is assessed in all settings.
whyNot.3: Lying and standing BP is part of the cardiovascular examination in all settings.

explain.body: CT within 1 hour for a GCS of 12 or less initially, GCS under 15 at 2 hours, skull fracture signs, seizure, focal deficit or more than one vomit. On an anticoagulant or antiplatelet (not aspirin alone) with no other indication: consider CT within 8 hours, or within 1 hour if presenting after 8 hours.

test.q: Mrs Kerr, 70, takes no anticoagulants. After a fall on the ward she has vomited twice and her GCS is 15. What does NICE NG232 advise?
options: CT head scan within 1 hour
CT head scan within 8 hours
Observe, as her GCS is 15
CT head scan within 24 hours
test.why: NG232 rec 1.5.8: more than one episode of vomiting after a head injury is a risk factor for a CT head scan within 1 hour.

whyNot.1: 8 hours applies to anticoagulation or LOC/amnesia with other factors; vomiting more than once needs CT within 1 hour.
whyNot.2: A normal GCS does not outweigh repeated vomiting.
whyNot.3: 24 hours is not the NG232 time frame for this risk factor.
